newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Farm Council agrees veterinary package.
newsitem.headline: Farm Council agrees veterinary package.

text.p: The Farm Council agreed on Tuesday a veterinary package consisting of the following measures, the Irish EU Presidency said.

- NEW ZEALAND: An agreement for the mutual recognition of EU and New Zealand veterinary and animal health controls was signed on Tuesday (See TRADE-NEW ZEALAND). Progress was noted in negotiations for similar agreements with the Australia and other major EU trading partners.

- SOMATOSALM: The Commission can on January 2, 1997, adopt a measure exempting maximum residue levels for the salmon growth promoter, somatosalm, after the EU Regulatory Committee did not support it and ministers failed to take a decision within the prescribed time limit.
The proposal amends annex II to Regulation 2377/90 for fixing maximum residue limits of veterinary medicinal products in animal food.

- BALAI DIRECTIVE: Ministers adopted rules to simplify animal and public health requirements under the so-called Balai Directive 118/92 for imports of animal products which have not been harmonised in the EU. The aim is to avoid difficulties at the start of 1997 due to the fact that a list of approved factories has not yet been drawn up for several of the products.
Member states agreed that imports of casings -- intestinal offal used to make sausage skins -- should continue under national rules.
- CATTLE REGISTER: Ministers asked COREPER to finalise a text amending Directive 432/64 to set up a register for dealers and transporters of cattle and pigs so as to improve health standards.

- VET CERTIFICATES: A regulation was adopted fixing rules for veterinary certificates. Non-EU countries are required to apply the same certificate standards for animals and produce destined for the EU.

- PRE-LISTING: Council decision 408/95, which expires at the end of 1996, has been extended until the end of 1998. It authorises the Commission to use a simplified system for approving non-EU establishments in advance of inspections. Non-EU countries must provide guarantees that they meet EU standards.

- PLANTS: Legal texts amending Council Directive 93/77 on protective measures against imports of organisms that may harm plants or plant products will be adopted at the next Farm Council in January. The seven-years-old proposal allows EU aid for member states to meet the cost of combating contamination from imports of plant-damaging organisms from another member state. But the aid must be refunded if compulsory plant health inspections are not carried out properly by the exporting member state.
- POTATOES: A regulation was agreed extending the protection of potato plant breeders' rights by five years to a total of 30 years as is the case for vine and tree species.
